articles.title: Building the Future of Japanese Tech Talent
articles.text:
Building the Future of Japanese Tech Talent
Hilary Carter | 28 August 2026
At the Linux Foundation, our community thrives because of the dedicated work of developers, project maintainers, enterprise partners, platform engineers, and generous sponsors worldwide. On behalf of the team at LF Research, I want to extend our heartfelt thanks to all of our global sponsors and partners whose continued support makes our research, open source initiatives, and educational programs possible.
Following KubeCon/CloudNativeCon Japan last month, Clyde Seepersad, Senior Vice President and General Manager of Linux Foundation Education, and I each gave a presentation in Tokyo rooted in recent research. Clyde’s talk described emerging trends unfolding across the Japanese tech talent ecosystem. Amid global conversations around automation and AI-driven efficiency, Japan stands out for its commitment to workforce development. While headlines elsewhere focus on potential job displacement, new research reveals that Japan leads globally in entry level hiring and structured onboarding. However, as AI adoption accelerates, Japan has a critical opportunity to build on this foundational strength by expanding continuous training across all seniority levels.
Our recent research publication, the 2026 State of Tech Talent Japan Report: Expanding Headcount and Closing the Skills Gap to Modernize Japan's Infrastructure, provides a comprehensive look at how Japanese organizations are navigating AI integration, infrastructure modernization, and talent retention.
Here is the story behind the data and what it means for the future of open source and enterprise technology in Japan.
AI creates jobs, but reveals a full-stack readiness challenge
A common worry surrounding artificial intelligence is that automation will shrink technical teams. The report demonstrates that the reality in Japan is quite the opposite. AI is serving as a strong net driver of job creation across Japan's IT sector, with net hiring growth rates projected at +54% in 2026 and +35% in 2027—substantially higher than global averages.
The entry level edge: Building pipelines from the ground up
One of the most encouraging findings from the report is Japan's unique approach to early career talent. While the rest of the world shows a negative net hiring effect for entry level technical roles (-2%), Japan shows a strongly positive net hiring effect of +46%.
This reflects a long-standing cultural strength in Japanese employment practices: bringing in promising talent, teaching them core business context, and developing their skill sets over time. When Clyde shared these insights with attendees in Tokyo, the resonance was clear. Japan’s ability to onboard junior engineers provides a solid base. To fully realize the benefits of modern technologies like cloud native computing, AI operations, and cybersecurity, this investment in learning must extend seamlessly to mid-career and senior engineers as well.
Bridging the gap in infrastructure and DevOps
Despite enthusiasm for AI, the report highlights significant capability gaps across critical infrastructure domains. Only 13% of Japanese organizations currently maintain dedicated AI and ML technical headcount, compared to 53% globally. The gap is even more pronounced in DevOps, CI/CD, and site reliability engineering, where only 18% of Japanese organizations have dedicated staff compared to 68% worldwide.
Furthermore, when asked about top barriers to realizing value from AI, Japanese organizations ranked a lack of infrastructure skills first (29%), whereas global peers cited security concerns as their primary obstacle. Without robust cloud, container, and SRE foundations, scaling AI workloads into reliable production systems remains difficult.
Why upskilling beats hiring for long-term growth
To bridge these skill gaps, Japanese enterprises are turning inward. The report shows that 54% of Japanese organizations prioritize hiring inexperienced professionals and upskilling them as their primary talent strategy. Across strategic technology domains, organizations are on average 9.3 times more likely to upskill existing employees than to hire externally.
This preference is grounded in practical economics and retention. The report reveals that hiring and onboarding new technical staff in Japan takes 81% longer than upskilling existing team members. Moreover, 46% of new external hires leave within six months—twice the global rate. By contrast, internal team members already understand the business domain and institutional culture, leading to higher quality work, faster time to productivity, and stronger staff retention.
When comparing workforce strategies directly, organizations report that upskilling outperforms hiring across every major operational measure, including quality of work, team cohesion, and overall retention.
Empowering tech talent across every career stage
Closing the skills gap requires sustained commitment across the entire open source ecosystem. For hiring managers and executive leaders, the report offers actionable takeaways:
- Invest in continuous internal training: Expand upskilling pathways beyond entry level onboarding to support senior and mid-level engineers as technologies evolve.
- Prioritize full-stack capability: Align training programs with cloud native infrastructure, container orchestration, DevOps, and AI security.
- Foster an open source culture: Granting dedicated open source contribution time and maintaining clear open source policies ranks second among effective retention strategies in Japan (88%), placing it above traditional compensation.
At the Linux Foundation, we remain dedicated to providing vendor-neutral certifications, training frameworks, and community programs that empower organizations and individuals alike. By building on Japan's established leadership in talent development and expanding training across every level of seniority, the technical community can successfully modernize infrastructure and unlock the full potential of AI.
Discover our library of insights
To read the complete findings, methodology, and detailed domain analysis, download your free copy of the 2026 State of Tech Talent Japan Report: Expanding Headcount and Closing the Skills Gap to Modernize Japan's Infrastructure.

Avec son gros tiroir de 6,2 litres, il joue dans une autre cour que les petits modèles pour une ou deux personnes. L’idée, c’est de préparer un vrai repas pour quatre sans rallumer le four, avec de quoi frire, rôtir, cuire, réchauffer et même déshydrater. Bon, forcément, ça prend un peu de place sur le plan de travail.
L’offre en cours sur le Ninja Air Fryer MAX PRO

- Six fonctions, dont Max Crisp jusqu’à 240 °C

Habituellement affiché à 149,99 euros, le Ninja Air Fryer MAX PRO revient à 99,99 euros sur Amazon. Soit 50 euros de moins, ce qui le place au niveau de modèles bien plus petits alors qu’on parle ici d’un tiroir de 6,2 litres.
Un tiroir taillé pour nourrir toute la famille
Dans la gamme Ninja, le MAX PRO occupe une place précise : c’est l’air fryer à simple tiroir le plus grand du catalogue, juste en dessous des modèles à double tiroir type Foodi Flex, plus chers et plus encombrants. Si vous n’avez pas besoin de deux paniers pour lancer deux cuissons en parallèle, ce tiroir unique évite de payer pour une fonction qu’on n’utilise pas forcément.
Le gros argument, c’est évidemment la capacité. Les 6,2 litres du tiroir carré peuvent accueillir jusqu’à quatre blancs de poulet ou environ 1 kg de frites, de quoi éviter les fournées à répétition quand on cuisine pour trois ou quatre convives. Le panier et la plaque de cuisson passent au lave-vaisselle, donc le nettoyage ne vire pas à la corvée.
En contrepartie, il faut lui trouver de la place : autour de 36 cm de large et près de 6 kg, ce n’est pas l’air fryer qu’on range et qu’on sort au quotidien. À réserver aux cuisines qui ont un peu de plan de travail disponible.
Six modes de cuisson et 2 000 W sous la main
Côté cuisson, le MAX PRO embarque une puissance de 2 000 watts et six fonctions : Frire sans huile, Max Crisp, Rôtir, Cuire au four, Réchauffer et Déshydrater. La fonction Max Crisp monte jusqu’à 240 °C, idéale pour rendre les surgelés bien croustillants en quelques minutes.
Ninja annonce jusqu’à 75 % de matières grasses en moins qu’avec des frites classiques et une belle économie d’énergie face à un four traditionnel. Le panneau numérique reste simple à prendre en main, même s’il faut parfois quelques essais pour trouver les bons temps de cuisson selon les plats.

articles.title: Por que o bocejo dos outros (e até a palavra) contagia você
articles.text:
Só ler ou pensar na palavra “bocejo” já é gatilho suficiente para fazer boa parte das pessoas bocejar. Não é força de expressão: o fenômeno é real, batizado por pesquisadores de contágio do bocejo, e acontece porque o cérebro processa a simples ideia de bocejar de um jeito parecido com o de ver alguém bocejando ao vivo.
O que ainda intriga a ciência é o motivo — por que bocejamos, para começo de conversa, e por que esse ato se espalha entre pessoas, e até entre espécies diferentes, com tanta facilidade.
Não existe consenso fechado sobre nenhuma das duas perguntas. Hoje, duas hipóteses concorrem para explicar a função biológica do bocejo, e uma terceira linha de pesquisa tenta entender por que ele contagia, ligando o fenômeno à proximidade social e à empatia, a capacidade de se colocar no lugar do outro.
Duas teorias, nenhuma vencedora
A hipótese mais conhecida é a do resfriamento cerebral. Segundo essa ideia, o bocejo — uma inspiração profunda seguida de abertura ampla da mandíbula — aumenta o fluxo de sangue e de ar para a região da cabeça, ajudando a baixar a temperatura do cérebro em momentos em que ele está menos eficiente, como no sono ou no tédio. Uma pesquisa de 2014 associada ao biólogo Andrew Gallup, da universidade estadunidense SUNY Oneonta, relaciona maior frequência de bocejos a ambientes mais quentes.
A segunda hipótese trata o bocejo como um regulador do estado de alerta. Por essa leitura, bocejar ajuda o cérebro a fazer transições entre níveis de vigilância — ao acordar, antes de dormir, ou na passagem do tédio para uma atividade que exige atenção. As duas explicações não são necessariamente excludentes: um bocejo pode resfriar o cérebro e, ao mesmo tempo, sinalizar uma mudança de estado de alerta. Nenhuma das duas é consenso fechado — ambas seguem sendo testadas.
Leia mais:
- Bocejo é contagioso? Veja o que a ciência tem a dizer
- Por que bocejamos ao ver alguém bocejar?
- Abrir a boca de sono ao ver outro bocejar é mais profundo do que parece
- Os animais também bocejam? Entenda o comportamento
Contágio tem a ver com empatia
A parte contagiosa do bocejo é estudada separadamente da função biológica dele. Um dos achados mais citados vem de pesquisadores da Universidade de Pisa (Itália), de 2011, que observaram que a chance de uma pessoa “pegar” o bocejo de outra aumenta conforme o vínculo social entre elas: familiares contagiam mais que amigos, que contagiam mais que conhecidos, que contagiam mais que estranhos.
A leitura mais aceita é que o contágio funciona como uma sincronização social automática, ligada à mesma rede cerebral usada para reconhecer e espelhar o estado emocional de quem está por perto.
Esse vínculo com a empatia, porém, é debatido. Alguns experimentos com pessoas no espectro autista relataram taxas menores de contágio, o que alimentou a hipótese de uma ligação direta entre bocejo contagioso e empatia — mas outros estudos não conseguiram repetir esse resultado, e a relação está longe de ser unânime entre pesquisadores da área.
Até cães bocejam ao ver humanos
O contágio também atravessa espécies. Um estudo de pesquisadores britânicos, publicado em 2008 na revista Biology Letters, mostrou cães bocejando com mais frequência depois de ver ou ouvir um humano bocejando, resultado interpretado na época como evidência de laços empáticos entre cães e seus tutores.
Trabalhos posteriores questionaram essa leitura: alguns não conseguiram reproduzir o efeito, e outros sugeriram que o bocejo do cachorro nessas situações pode estar mais ligado a estresse ou a uma resposta automática a estímulo do que propriamente à empatia.
Isso deixa a ciência do bocejo num ponto interessante: há dados sólidos mostrando que o fenômeno existe e se espalha, mas explicações concorrentes sobre o porquê. Se alguém bocejou lendo este texto até aqui, faz parte da estatística — e é um bom motivo para reparar, na próxima roda de amigos, quem contagia quem primeiro.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: I went to China to see a different AI future. It looked familiar
articles.text:
Gordon Saft is the Publisher of Rest of World. Last week, he returned to New York from a trip to China with a delegation of leaders from across media, technology, public policy, and finance to gain a deeper understanding of the AI and robotics industries.
On my first morning in Beijing, before joining a delegation trip on China’s AI and robotics industries, I visited an exhibition by the Belgian-born conceptual artist Carsten Höller, called “Two.” Visitors enter through one of two doors, assigned at random. One half of the space is a full-color replica of the other rendered entirely in black and white. Walking through it, everything felt familiar yet slightly off all at once.
The debate over AI in the U.S. has long felt oppositional and binary: open versus closed, diffusion versus frontier, LLMs versus world models. Underneath it is a bigger framing that treats the U.S. and China as two competing models for how AI should be built and deployed, racing toward different futures. I wanted to understand if this held up on the ground, 18 months after DeepSeek’s launch reshaped open-source AI.
The institutions and politics diverge significantly, and the technology carries risks neither country can wave away. I expected the differences to be what struck me. Instead, it was the similarities.
I’d made a few similar trips to European cities over the past year, and each left me rattled by conversations about stagnation and uncertainty, a pessimism about technology and growth more entrenched than anything in America’s own debates. China was the opposite. I came back to New York surprised by how familiar the dynamism and optimism felt.
One theme surfaced repeatedly: China’s intense focus on deploying AI into the physical world, in robotics, manufacturing, electric vehicles, and embodied intelligence. Whether that’s conviction or a response to American export controls depends on who you ask. One researcher argued chips aren’t the real constraint anymore, data is. If he’s right, the export control debate is fighting yesterday’s war. Even Washington’s strongest leverage hasn’t held: Last summer, restrictions on EDA software were relaxed within weeks as part of a trade deal tied to rare earths.
Xi Jinping’s recent speeches on AI are more nuanced and technically informed than many Western observers assume, several China experts told me before the trip, and Beijing has worked to present itself as a responsible steward of AI rather than a competitor. What surprised me more was how often AI safety came up in these conversations. One analyst described responsibility for AI safety as increasingly sitting inside China’s national security establishment, treating advanced AI as strategic capability first, consumer technology second. Additionally, China’s capacity to move quickly is inseparable from a political system that places far less weight on individual liberty, due process, and constraints on state power. The surveillance cameras on every block are impossible to ignore.
The more people I talked to, the less this looked like innovation versus regulation and the more it looked like two powers staring at different maps. In the U.S., the limit is frontier capability itself, plus the looming threat of rare-earth leverage. In China, the conversation kept returning to deployment, and how quickly powerful models could be embedded into everyday life. It’s why the LLM-versus-world-model debate feels alive in China. If embodied AI is the next frontier, the scarce resource may be high-quality interaction with the physical world rather than raw compute, and China is generating exactly that.
China’s focus on deployment appears to be intentional. Cut off from leading-edge chips, the country has leaned into ground it can still win: getting AI into factories, vehicles, and everyday life faster than anyone else. Whether that’s conviction or necessity may not matter. If embedding AI across an economy ends up mattering more than owning the best frontier model, China’s constraint may have become its strategy.
On my last night in Shanghai, I walked into the Huawei flagship store directly across from an Apple Store on Nanjing Road. Where a Genius Bar might be in an Apple Store, Huawei had filled the back with electric vehicles. I thought of the Xiaomi factory we’d visited earlier, a phone company that became one of China’s largest EV manufacturers in just a few years. We rode a trolley through a robotic assembly line like an attraction at Universal Studios, watching cars that looked like electric Porsches glide silently through production. Apple spent years trying to build a car before abandoning the effort; adapting consumer hardware manufacturing into EVs was the very thing Xiaomi had pulled off.
Höller’s exhibit stayed with me. Your sense of which side is real depends entirely on which door you entered through. Dizzyingly, China felt like that. Everywhere I turned, there was something familiar: a slightly more advanced smartphone, a robot-operated coffee shop, a sleek electric vehicle — each refracted through a different political system and a different bet on the future. The differences were expected; the similarities were the surprise.
